Welcome to the Strobily turntable calibrator. This is for calibrating your record-playing turntables. To begin, you\'ll need to attach a pattern to your turntable. A good start would be to search \"strobe calibrate turntable\" on Google.
Select the highest frequency that is green, then adjust your turntable until the pattern appears to stop moving.
Welcome to the Strobily widget creator. This page allows you to set any of your saved patterns as widgets that you can click on your homescreen. \n\nTo begin, select a pattern:

This part of the app uses sound to identify the frequency of a spinning object. To use it, find a spinning object that is making a sound and press one of the four buttons to take a sound sample. 

When the results appear, the first number is the frequency that was identified and the other buttons represent fractions of that frequency. The greener a button is, the stronger that frequency was identified. (However if they're all green, most likely no match was found.) Normal-colored buttons did not rank in the top 5. 

If your spinning object is not making a sound, you may have to intervene. An example would be sticking a playing card into a fan in order to make a repeating sound. 

The Strobe Frequency Offset allows you to flash at a slightly different frequency than your spinning object such that it will appear to slowly spin. This value is only applied when you select a frequency (it doesn't affect detection).

This graph show what the app was doing during the past 100 flashes. The x-axis width is set so that it exactly matches the frequency of the strobe. 

Think of each row as 1 bar of music. The LED needs to turn fully-on and fully-off within 1 bar to keep up with the tempo. If the tempo is too fast, the LED falls behind and isn't able to turn on and off before the next row starts. 

Perfect performance will be a white vertical line. Diagonal lines mean it's not keeping up.

This is a mode that turns your phone into a signal generator. Instead of flashing the LED or the screen, the intent is that you would flash a device hooked up to your phone via the headphone jack and then probably some more electronics. 

Your phone really isn't designed to do this, so there are some considerations: 
• The voltages on this screen aren't real voltages. They are just the max and minimum value that one can specify. I find that they do in fact come out close to 1V and -1V when I measure it, but that also depends on system volume and your dongle etc. 
• Not all dongles will work! I tested two I own. A generic JSAUX and an apple one. The apple one does not work well. More on this below. 
• Perhaps this is obvious, but be careful hooking your phone up to electronics. An optical isolator might be wise. 

Some dongles have what's called an AC bias, basically the output waveform is going to be centered around 0 volts. Presumably this is good for audio, but it's bad for control signals. You want a dongle that can output a constant DC voltage. If you have one of the AC-biased ones, the voltages will decay to 0 on the order of a second. 

Thankfully, it's easy to test this! Hook a multimeter up to the output of the headphone jack (cut up an old pair of headphones if you need to). Ground to ground, positive to one of the signal wires. With the app in AUX mode, press the "Torch" button in the bottom left. This will output the high voltage. Press it again, this will output the low voltage. Now here's the key, if you have a compatible dongle, when it outputs the high voltage, it will stay there indefinitely. So for instance, it might output 1.1V and stay there. If you have an incompatible dongle, it will output 1.1V but will immediately decay to 0 within about a second. Assuming your Low voltage is set to 0 in the app, turning torch mode off will go back to 0 on a good dongle, or go to -1.1V and decay back to 0 on an incompatible dongle. 

Having tested only 2 dongles myself, I suspect that cheaper dongles are more likely to be compatible than expensive ones. I think the AC bias is likely a bit more hardware.
Control equipment connected to your phone via the headphone jack. Not all dongles work the same. Find one that passes DC current. Enable at bottom of screen
